extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (Analysis I) and novices learning how to construct proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for discovering, structuring, and memorizing routine Analysis I proofs by using a small set of standard proof 'moves' and bookkeeping techniques. Emphasises algorithmic, epsilon-N style strategies and when to expand definitions or pick specific witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimise use of memory / remember structure, not symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Make as little use of your memory as you possibly can; aim for a memory of a proof to be a structured pattern rather than a string of symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: instead of memorising a long symbol string, notice patterns (54321 87654321). Similarly, remember the routine pattern of steps and only memorise the occasional non-obvious step; understanding why the non-obvious step is sensible makes memorization much easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep doing the obvious thing
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Analysis I proofs are solved by repeatedly doing the obvious elementary steps until a small idea is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you 'just repeatedly do the obvious thing' you will often solve the problem; experienced mathematicians see many steps as 'obvious' that beginners view as hard. Train yourself to carry out routine simplifications and checks automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equip yourself with a small set of proof 'moves' and apply them
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn a compact repertoire of standard moves (let, naming, expansion, substitution, etc.) and consciously apply them when opportunities arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being aware of the moves is useful; avoid applying them in 'silly' ways (humans can usually recognise silliness). The blog demonstrates these moves by constructing the Cauchy/subsequence convergence proof step-by-step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record assumptions above a line and goals below the line
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep track of what you are allowed to assume (listed above a horizontal line) and what you are trying to prove (listed below the line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This bookkeeping technique helps you see which statements change during discovery and which statements you can use; it is useful when you are learning but not necessarily required forever.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'let' move
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving 'For every X such that P(X) holds, Q(X) also holds', write 'Let X be such that P(X) holds' and change the target to proving Q(X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'let' move to eliminate universal quantifiers in the target and reduce the proof to a particular but arbitrary object satisfying the hypothesis; applied repeatedly in the example proof to handle quantifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'naming' move
rubrics_metrics.description: When you are told that something exists (e.g., a subsequence or a limit), give it a name and record its properties explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: given 'has a convergent subsequence', name it (a_nk) and list 'is a subsequence of (a_n)' and 'converges'; then name its limit L. Naming clarifies what the hypotheses actually provide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion (expand definitions when stuck)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you cannot find a high-level argument, rephrase the target using low-level definitions (often involving quantifiers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid expanding definitions unless genuinely stuck so you don't miss opportunities to use course results instead of reproving basics. Expansion is useful when the statement involves convergence, continuity, Cauchy, etc.; e.g., replace 'converges' by its epsilon-N definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: You must know precise definitions to be able to expand targets and hypotheses usefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without precise knowledge of definitions you cannot perform expansion moves; the example emphasises that knowing the epsilon-N definitions is vital to carry out low-level proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution into a hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a hypothesis of the form 'for all x, if conditions C(x) then R(x)', and given a particular object t of the appropriate type, substitute t for x to obtain C(t) implies R(t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog labels this substitution and likens it to modus ponens in practice. Example: from 'is Cauchy' in expanded form you can substitute a particular epsilon or N to get a concrete inequality; after substitution one often 'names' the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modus ponens (use hypotheses with conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a hypothesis says 'whenever you can find x satisfying conditions C, you can assert R', use that by finding (or choosing) an x that meets C and then conclude R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post frames this as using conditional/implicational hypotheses: find a witness that satisfies the conditions and then take the consequent as available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution into a target (choose a witness for an existential)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the target is existential ('there exists y such that S(y)'), and you have a candidate y in mind, change the target to proving S(candidate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This removes existential quantifiers and turns the problem into proving the property for the chosen explicit object (e.g., choose L as the limit to prove the whole sequence converges to L).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing parameters to make tools apply (e.g., pick epsilons, Ns)
rubrics_metrics.description: When you need two-step closeness or several conditions, pick parameter values (like epsilons and indices) to satisfy the requirements of the hypotheses and tools you plan to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example strategy: if you need |a_n - L| < eps and plan to use triangle inequality via a subsequence, take eps/2 and choose indices so both pieces are < eps/2. Choose N as max of other Ns; pick values so the hypotheses' preconditions hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer using course results over reproving from first principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Before expanding to low-level definitions, check whether a higher-level result from the course applies; use it rather than doing everything from first principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expanding definitions repeatedly can hide easier routes; use known theorems to keep proofs simpler and avoid unnecessary technical expansions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise and avoid 'silly' applications of moves
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying moves mechanically can lead to unhelpful or 'silly' reasoning steps; aim to apply moves sensibly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although moves are algorithmic, human judgement is needed to spot when a move is pointless or leads to circular/inefficient work. Experience helps recognise 'silliness'.
